title: The new wine (Luke 5:27–39)
hookLine: Levi's big feast, and no one after drinking old wine wants new
last: WE HAVE SEEN STRANGE THINGS TODAY.

lines: A TAX BOOTH BY THE ROAD.
cards: A tax booth on a road near the lake. Levi sits behind it, collecting customs on goods passing through. Steady money, and it does not make him popular.
Earlier in Luke, John the Baptist tells tax collectors to collect no more than they're owed, which says something about their reputation. Jesus walks up and says two words: "Follow me."

And Luke says, "he left all, rose up, and followed him." No negotiation. Then Levi does what people do when their life changes overnight: he throws a big party in his own house and invites everyone he knows.
For a tax collector, that means a lot of other tax collectors.

teach.b: Some Pharisees and their scribes ask the disciples: "Why do ye eat and drink with publicans and sinners?" For them, a shared table was a sign of belonging, and they took holiness seriously.

Jesus answers: "They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." Then they ask about fasting: John's disciples fast, yours eat and drink.
Jesus answers with pictures from the kitchen. Nobody tears a patch from a new coat to fix an old one.
Nobody pours new wine into old wineskins: "else the new wine will burst the bottles, and be spilled." Bottles here are wineskins, leather bags.

New wine is still fermenting, still stretching; an old skin, already stiff, can't give, and it splits. "But new wine must be put into new bottles; and both are preserved." Something new needs room to grow.

teach.h: THE OLD IS BETTER, PEOPLE SAY.
teach.b: Then a last line, almost a joke: "No man also having drunk old wine straightway desireth new: for he saith, The old is better." We like what we know.
Readers have heard this many ways: some as gentle patience with people slow to change, others as a wry smile at how hard change is.

teach.h: NEW WINE MUST BE PUT INTO NEW BOTTLES.
teach.b: Levi changed overnight. Others take longer. The text seems to make room for both.

how: Christians remember Levi as Matthew, the tax collector who became an apostle, and many churches read the call of Levi as a picture of welcome at the table.

games.q: you're Levi. a teacher walks up to your tax booth and says: follow me. what do you do?
o: leave everything, get up, and follow, then throw a feast.
games.why: Levi leaves all and follows, then throws a great feast in his own house for everyone he knows.

practice: Think of something new you've wanted to start, a few minutes of quiet in the morning, a walk, an earlier bedtime, and notice the part of you that says the old way is fine; that's not a villain, just old wine talking.
Picture the smallest new skin you could make room for, one minute instead of thirty, something that can stretch as it grows.
If you pray, you can ask for patience with your own pace; if you don't, simply let the small new thing feel welcome.

wordCard.voice: Wineskins. The leather bags Jesus says new wine needs: old ones, already stretched stiff, split; new ones give the wine room to grow.

orig.note: Greek: a wineskin, a leather bag. the "bottles" of the King James Bible.

carryVoice: Your line: new wine takes time. Slow change still counts as change. That's day five hundred twenty-one.
